Books · Instrumentation Symbols and Identification · Chapter 7

Drawings — worked examples

ANSI/ISA-5.1-1984 (R1992) · §§6.9–6.12

Chapter 7 · 17 source pages · 17 figures · companion notes
Key terms. Function example — one letter combination placed in a typical loop. · Complex combination — a diagram combining several symbol families on one process. · PLC — programmable logic controller, the diamond-in-a-square symbol. · Purge / safety purging — instrument purging for protection or for safe operation. · Degree of detail — simplified / conceptual / detailed, user-chosen but required to stay consistent.

The first six chapters built the vocabulary: definitions, tag numbers, identification letters and 20 symbol sheets. This final chapter is the grammar — 17 example sheets from page 48 to page 64, where those symbols are assembled into loops, interlock schemes and complete drawings. It is also the most-used chapter in practice: when you need to know how an FRC or a PLC diamond should be drawn, you turn to clauses 6.9–6.12.

How to read the examples What the standard warns first

«This usage does not imply, however, that the applications or designations of the instruments or functions are restricted in any way. No inference should be drawn that the choice of any of the schemes for illustration constitutes a recommendation for the illustrated methods of measurement or control.»

ANSI/ISA-5.1-1984 (R1992), clause 4.4.1
  1. Examples are not recommendations. Alternative symbols are shown side by side without a stated preference; their relative order does not imply one (4.4.1).
  2. The bubble has two roles. It either represents the instrument itself or acts as a tag attached to a distinctive symbol such as a control valve — in that case the connecting line is drawn close to, but not touching, the symbol (4.4.2).
  3. Not every element needs a tag. An orifice flange or a control valve may be left untagged when its relationship to the loop is obvious; showing a primary-element symbol is likewise optional (4.4.3).
  4. Short notes remove ambiguity. The notations 3–9 psig and 9–15 psig beside signal lines, combined with the failure-mode symbols, fully define a split-range valve pair (4.4.4).
  5. Symbol orientation is free, lettering is not. Symbols may be rotated and signal lines may enter or leave at any angle; only Table 3 function-block designators and tag numbers stay horizontal. Directional arrowheads are recommended on complex drawings (4.4.6).
  6. Diagrams show logic, not wiring. The connection order must reflect information flow even though voltage loops are wired in parallel and current loops in series; both are drawn as parallel so the diagram stays independent of the installed hardware (4.4.9).
  7. Degree of detail is the user's choice. Sketches are usually highly simplified and process flow diagrams less detailed than engineering flow diagrams; what is mandatory is consistency for each application (4.4.10).

Reading a loop from its tag number A guided example

Before the sheets, walk through one typical flow-control loop. The table below reuses exactly the rules of Chapters 3–5: the first letter is the measured variable, succeeding letters are the functions, the numeric part is the loop number, and the position of the bubble on the drawing tells you where the device is mounted.

TagRead asSymbol on drawing
FE-1E = primary element, F = flowOrifice plate in the process line; a separate bubble is optional (4.4.3).
FT-1T = transmitter, F = flowPlain field-mounted circle (no horizontal bar), joined by a fine signal line.
FRC-1R = record, C = control, F = flowCircle with a horizontal bar at the primary location, accessible to the operator (6.3).
FAL-1 / FAH-1A = alarm, L / H = low / highL / H written beside the bubble; the pilot light uses its own clause 6.3 symbol.
FV-1V = valve, F = flowValve body (6.4) + actuator (6.5) + an FC / FO failure symbol (6.7).

An FRC-1 loop read in information-flow order rather than wiring order.

Reading tip. Follow the arrowheads left to right: primary element → transmitter → function (bubble) → final actuator. Whenever you meet a circle inside a square, a hexagon or a diamond, go back to the 3×4 matrix in Chapter 6 to decide whether it is a computer function, shared control or programmable logic.

6.9 · Examples — functions The standard's example sheets

The first eight example sheets apply one function at a time to a typical loop: indicating, recording, controlling, auto–manual control stations, high/low alarms, switches and interlock relays, pilot lights, computing devices (sum, ratio, integrate/totalize, scan, limiters), transmitters, test points, viewing glasses, hand operation, drivers and multifunction combinations. This is where Table 1 (Chapter 4) and Table 2 (Chapter 5) become pictures: each letter combination sits in a bubble, on a signal line, connected to a primary element and a valve. Read each example by walking from the tag number through the bubble, along the signal line and out to the final element — that order is the information flow of the loop.

6.10 · Examples — miscellaneous combinations The standard's example sheets

Five more sheets place side by side the combinations that do not fit neatly into one function class: programmable logic controllers (PLC), purge and safety-purging arrangements, data links, shared display / shared control devices, and the ways of adding information by notes adjacent to a symbol. Note how the diamond-in-a-square (programmable logic function) connects directly to binary signals while the bubbles still follow the clause 6.3 convention. These examples also illustrate clause 4.4.11: intermediate interlock hardware (auxiliary relays, current transformers) may be omitted from engineering flow diagrams and shown on another document.

6.11 · Example — complex combinations The standard's example sheets

A single sheet, but the densest in clause 6: one diagram combining a primary element, transmitter, computing function, shared display / shared control, programmable logic, binary interlocks, an actuator and its power-failure state. It is the practical test of the whole symbol system — if you can read this sheet, you have seen how the rules of the earlier chapters work together. The standard recommends directional arrowheads on signal lines in drawings this complex (clause 4.4.6), to make information flow clear independently of the actual wiring.

Sheet 14 · standard page 61

6.12 · Example — degree of detail The standard's example sheets

The final three sheets draw the same process at three levels of detail: simplified, conceptual and detailed. These are not three different document types but a cross-section showing that one symbol system can contract or expand to suit the purpose — exactly as clause 4.4.10 states: the degree of detail is entirely at the user's discretion, and the only requirement is consistency within each application. The simplified version may be a handful of bubbles; the detailed one exposes in-line components, test points, split-range notations and failure symbols. Closing clause 6, this is also its most important reminder: symbols are the language, and the writer chooses how long the sentence is.

6.12 · Three levels of detail One process, three renderings

Standard termLevel of detailTypical use
SimplifiedA few bubbles and signal lines; most off-line detail omitted.Design sketches, technical papers, teaching examples.
ConceptualShows the functional relationships between loops without enumerating every element.Process flow diagrams, functional descriptions, system overviews.
DetailedFull in-line components, test points, split-range notes and power-failure states.Engineering flow diagrams / P&IDs, construction and loop wiring documents.

From clause 4.4.10 and sheets 62–64; these three names represent a cross-section of symbol usage, not three mandatory document types.

  • Sheets 62–64 depict the same process, so the difference between them is only the level of detail, not a difference in equipment or process scheme.
  • The standard does not prescribe how detailed any particular drawing must be; each user sets the level suited to the document's purpose and then holds it steady across the document set.
  • This is why the example sheets of 6.9–6.11 should be read as usage demonstrations rather than templates that must be copied.

Closing the standard From letters to a complete drawing

The book's seven chapters follow one line: purpose and scope (Chapter 1) → definitions (Chapter 2) → tag-number structure (Chapter 3) → identification letters (Chapter 4) → letter combinations and function blocks (Chapter 5) → 20 symbol sheets (Chapter 6) → the 17 example sheets here. With the four Table 3 function-block sheets in Chapter 5, all 41 vector sheets of clauses 5.4 and 6 are reproduced in full, plus two redrawn figures for Figure 1 and the six core SAMA blocks.

  1. Clause 3 — Definitions: see Chapter 2.
  2. Clause 4 — Identification system and Figure 1: see Chapter 3.
  3. Clause 5.1 — Table 1 identification letters and its 22 notes: see Chapter 4.
  4. Clauses 5.2–5.4 — Tables 2 and 3 and SAMA function blocks: see Chapter 5.
  5. Clauses 6.1–6.8 — 20 sheets of line, bubble, valve, actuator and primary-element symbols: see Chapter 6.
About this reproduction. The example sheets in the source PDF have no text layer — every line and label is a vector drawing operator. Each sheet here is replayed directly as SVG <path> elements, preserving the standard's layout and its original English labels; the paired Vietnamese caption explains the content. The Vietnamese translation renders the full normative prose, while labels inside the figures are kept verbatim so readers can check them against ANSI/ISA-5.1-1984 (R1992).
